text: You run a lemonade stand. Each lemonade costs five dollars. Customers line up and pay one at a time, with a five, a ten, or a twenty dollar bill. You have to give correct change, so each customer pays five dollars in the end. You start with no change at all. Return true if you can give every customer correct change.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I only have the bills that earlier customers gave me. I can't borrow from a customer who is still in line. So the order of the bills matters, and I must be able to pay change at every step, not just in total. Is that right?
Yes. Change has to be paid right away, with what you have right now.

Okay. One more observation. Change only ever comes in two shapes. A ten needs five back. A twenty needs fifteen back, which is either ten plus five, or three fives. I never hand out a twenty, so I don't need to count twenties at all — just fives and tens. Are there any constraints on the input size?
The array has up to ten to the fifth bills, and every bill is a five, a ten, or a twenty.

Got it. Up to a hundred thousand customers, so I want one pass. Quick check on the example: five, five, five, ten, twenty. The only moment that matters is the twenty — by then I hold two fives and a ten, so I give back the ten and a five. Everyone got change, so true. That matches.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try both ways of giving change at every twenty and search all the choices. That branches at every twenty, so it grows exponentially — way too slow for a hundred thousand customers. This problem reminds me of a greedy coin choice. The only real decision is at a twenty: ten plus five, or three fives. A five is the more useful bill — it can pay change for a ten and for a twenty, while a ten only helps with a twenty. So I spend the ten and keep my fives. That turns it into a simple simulation with two counters.

Here's the plan. One: keep two counters, pay five and pay ten, for the bills I hold. Two: a five, keep it; a ten, hand back a five; a twenty, hand back a ten plus a five if I have a ten, otherwise three fives. Three: the moment pay five would go below zero, fail on the spot. One thing worth flagging — why give the ten first? Take four fives, then a ten, a twenty, and another ten. At the twenty, greedy keeps two fives, while three fives first keeps none. So the last ten gets no change, and only greedy survives — a ten can't do anything a five can't. Also, failing inside the loop is a correctness rule: an end-only check would pass ten then five. Greedy is linear time, constant space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop with two counters. A five bumps pay five; a ten spends a five; a twenty spends a ten and a five if I hold a ten, else three fives — and any time pay five dips below zero, I return false right away. If the loop finishes, I return true. One thing worth flagging — in the twenty branch, if I have a ten but no five, I return false without falling back to three fives. That's correct: the fallback needs three fives and I have zero. And the check is strictly below zero, not below or equal — landing on exactly zero fives is fine.

Let's dry-run the code. Five, five, ten, ten, twenty — expected false. The row that matters is the twenty: the two tens already used up both fives, so I hold two tens and zero fives. I hand back a ten, pay five goes to negative one, and I return false on the spot. Fifteen dollars of change always needs a five. That matches. Corner cases: a single ten or twenty is false, since the first customer must pay with a five. Ten then five is false — exactly where an end-only check would wrongly say true. Five then ten is true, landing on zero fives. Three fives then a twenty is true, through the three-fives branch.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one look at each bill, a few constant-time updates each. Space is constant — just two counters. The worst case is when everyone can be paid, so the loop runs to the end; any failure stops earlier. Oh, one more thing — the greedy choice is the only smart part, so I'd test it hardest, by comparing against the brute force that tries both ways at every twenty, on lots of short inputs.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw early that only fives and tens matter, and that the order of customers matters. You proved give-the-ten-first with a real counterexample, instead of just saying greedy. And you showed the early return is about correctness, not speed — plus why the check is strictly below zero, not below or equal. Good work.
